## August 24, 1931 — A Monday

You were born on a Monday in the worst economic catastrophe the modern world had yet produced. The Great Depression was not approaching in August 1931. It was already there, fully arrived, and deepening. American unemployment was climbing toward fifteen percent on its way to twenty-five. Banks were failing by the hundreds. Farms were failing. The bread lines were not a metaphor. The world you entered was one in which the assumptions of the previous decade — prosperity, growth, the permanent forward march of modern economies — had collapsed without warning and showed no signs of recovering.

---

**Your birthday is August 24th, and on August 24th in the year 79, Mount Vesuvius destroyed Pompeii.** Across the Roman Empire that day, life continued as normal. In Pompeii and Herculaneum, it ended by afternoon. The eruption buried cities so completely that they were lost for fifteen centuries, preserved by catastrophe, rediscovered by accident. When you were born, the ruins of Pompeii had been under excavation for nearly two hundred years and were still yielding their dead — plaster casts of human forms caught in their final moments, preserved by the ash that killed them. You share a calendar date with the most famous volcanic disaster in Western history, across a distance of 1,852 years.

**And on August 24th, 1814 — exactly 117 years before your birth — the British Army burned Washington.** It remains the only time since the Revolution that a foreign power captured and torched the American capital. The White House, the Capitol, the Library of Congress — set alight and left smoldering. President Madison had already fled. The memory of that humiliation was still living history to some grandparents of your grandparents' generation. Your birthday carries it as an anniversary.

**The Empire State Building had been open for less than four months.** It opened on May 1, 1931, and when you were born it was still the newest wonder in New York's skyline, still the tallest structure in the world — a title it would hold for forty years. There is something characteristic about 1931 in that fact: that the same year produced both the Empire State Building and breadlines stretching around city blocks. The Depression did not stop ambition or construction or grandeur. It simply made them coexist with devastation.

**Twenty-five days after your birth, Japan invaded Manchuria.** On September 18, 1931, the Japanese Kwantung Army staged an incident on a railway line near Mukden and used it as a pretext to seize control of Manchuria. The League of Nations condemned the action and did nothing. It was the first major act of military aggression that would, through the following decade, lead directly to the Second World War. You were not yet a month old when the chain of events began that would define your entire childhood and adolescence.

**Adolf Hitler was not yet in power.** In August 1931, the Nazi Party had made dramatic gains in the September 1930 elections and was the second-largest party in the German parliament, but Hitler was still seventeen months from becoming Chancellor. The Germany you were born into was a democracy in crisis — Weimar's democracy, fragile, hyperinflated in memory, politically unstable, but still standing. The world that became the Holocaust and the Second World War had not yet arrived. It was gathering. You were born in the last interval before it was inevitable.

**Britain was days from abandoning the gold standard.** The financial crisis gripping Britain in August 1931 culminated on September 21st — less than a month after your birth — when the British government suspended the gold standard, a monetary anchor that had organized the global economy for decades. The economic world of your parents and grandparents was dissolving in real time in the weeks around your arrival.

---

**The arc of a lifetime.**

You are ninety-five years old as of 2026. There is almost no framework for what that span contains.

You were born before commercial aviation was common, before television existed, before penicillin was in use, before the atom had been split. You were a child during the Depression and an adolescent during World War II — the war was declared when you were eight years old in Europe, ten when Pearl Harbor brought America in, thirteen when the tide turned at Stalingrad and in the Pacific, thirteen when the D-Day landings happened, and thirteen still when the atomic bombs fell on Hiroshima and Nagasaki and the war ended. Your entire childhood was shaped by catastrophe: the Depression and then the war, one following directly from the other.

You were thirty-two when Kennedy was assassinated. Thirty-seven when humans first walked on the moon. Fifty-eight when the Berlin Wall fell — old enough to have lived your entire adult life through the Cold War and to see its end while still in middle age. Seventy when September 11th happened. Eighty-eight when a global pandemic reorganized the world.

The technologies that define daily life in 2026 — smartphones, the internet, streaming, social media, GPS navigation — did not exist until your sixties or later. You have watched the world not merely change but transform, repeatedly and completely, across a span of time in which multiple historical eras have risen and ended.

Born into the Depression, shaped by a world war, outlasting the Cold War, still present as artificial intelligence reshapes the economy: ninety-five years of a world that has not stopped moving since the Monday in August when you arrived in the middle of its worst breakdown.
